Ranches, Raids, and the Rangers

Round-up scenes on the Belle Fourche, 1887. Photograph by John Grabill, Library of Congress. Public domain (cropped).
Mini-lesson · Mr. Peregrin

Life at the Edge

Today's Focus

A ranch on the edge of Texas was a farm, a fort, and a target all at once.

Before the Civil War, a family on the edge of Texas could lose its horses in a night. Another family, farther south, might lose its land to a lawsuit. You will see what life was like on frontier ranches, how raids and border trouble tested them, and what the Rangers did and did not do about it.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to…
  1. describe what frontier ranches in the Hill Country and South Texas were like.
  2. explain what caused trouble along the Rio Grande in the 1850s.
  3. describe who the Texas Rangers were, how they worked, and what they did on the frontier.

Part 1

Life on the Edge

Chapter 1Ranches at the Edge
Chapter 1

Ranches at the Edge

In the 1850s, two parts of Texas stood at the edge of the frontier. One was the Hill Country, where German farmers and Anglo ranchers raised cattle in the valleys. The other was South Texas, between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande. There, Mexican and Tejano families had run ranchos since Spanish times. Newcomers like Richard King and Mifflin Kenedy were building huge ranches on the same ground. Both areas were open grassland with few fences, and the cattle ran on land no one had ever walked off.

Settlement followed the water. In the 1850s the line of farms and ranches crept west across the Hill Country and the plains south of it, one creek at a time. A family looked for a spring or a river with grass nearby, then built close by. The headquarters usually had a house, a corral for the horses, pens for working cattle, and perhaps a shed for saddles and tools. Ranches sat far apart. The land between them was open range, and cattle from several ranches mixed and wandered across it. That is why brands were recorded in county books, so that at the next round-up, neighbors could sort out whose animals were whose.

South Texas worked a little differently. The old Spanish and Mexican ranchos there had been large, and their owners kept big herds on land that stretched for miles. In 1853, Richard King set up a camp on Santa Gertrudis Creek in the brush country. He added land, bought cattle, and brought in the Mexican families who knew how to work them. In time his place became the King Ranch, one of the largest in the world. Mifflin Kenedy, King’s friend and business partner, built a ranch of his own in the same region.

In the Hill Country, neighbors were often very different from one another. A German farmer with stone fences might live a few miles from a Southern rancher with open-range cattle and a few Mexican hands. They traded, borrowed tools, and helped one another when a barn burned or a horse was lost. A community might have a store, a mill, and a church, and ranch families rode in on the weekend.

Life on such a ranch was hard. A house might be built of stone or heavy timber, with few windows. The nearest neighbor could be miles away. Men rode for days to gather cattle, and during that time women and children were often left to protect the house. A family’s wealth was its herd and its horses, and both could be taken in a single night.

A year on a ranch had its own rhythm. Spring was round-up season, when riders gathered the herd, counted it, and branded the new calves. Summer meant keeping cattle near water and looking for animals lost in the brush. In fall and winter, a rancher decided which animals to sell. Cattle went to market on foot, in herds, to ports on the Gulf coast and to markets in Louisiana. A herd might walk for weeks to reach a buyer.

Horses were the other half of the business. Young horses had to be caught, gentled, and taught to carry a saddle, and then taught to follow a cow. A rancher wanted a string of horses so that no one animal worked too long. A rider on a worn-out horse could not do the job, and a horse that went lame could leave its rider stranded miles from help.

Ranch houses were built from whatever was close by. In the Hill Country that meant limestone, which settlers cut into blocks, or cedar logs. In the brush country, builders used timber posts and adobe, a brick made of earth and straw. Thick walls kept the rooms cool in summer, and small windows were easier to defend.

Picture a family in a small rock house in the 1850s on a morning in early spring. The father and two hired riders saddle up before sunrise to start the round-up. The mother checks the corral, counts the horses, and puts a rifle by the door. The children carry water. Nothing about the day is unusual. That is what ranch life was: work that started in the dark, with the animals always in sight.

Ranch families depended on one another. They traveled in groups, shared news, and came to help when a neighbor needed it. They also relied on the Texas Rangers, and on the soldiers in the nearest fort, though neither was ever close enough.

Part 2

Raids

Chapter 2Raids on the Frontier
Chapter 3The Texas Rangers
Chapter 2

Raids on the Frontier

In the Hill Country, the danger came from raiders from several Native peoples, most often Comanche and Lipan Apache. Their most common target was horses. Horses were wealth, and a ranch with fine horses was a prize. Raids could also be deadly. People were killed, and some were carried off as captives. Settlers lived with the fear of it, and they pressed the state government to send help.

To see why horses were the prize, you have to know how the Comanche lived. They had been horse people for more than a century, and they were among the best riders on the continent. A Comanche warrior could ride at a full gallop, hang along the side of his horse to use it as cover, and shoot a bow from under its neck. Horses gave him speed, and a big herd meant wealth.

Raiders often struck at night. Many Texans spoke of a “Comanche moon,” a bright full moon that made it easy to travel after dark. Raiders would take horses from a corral or pasture, drive them off fast, and be miles away by dawn. Settlers learned to take care. They penned their best horses near the house at night, kept dogs, and set a watch. Neighbors rode together to follow a trail.

The army helped too. In the late 1840s and the 1850s, it built a chain of forts along the frontier, including Fort Martin Scott near Fredericksburg and Fort Mason farther west. But soldiers on foot had a hard time catching riders on fast horses, so the army also turned to mounted troops.

Picture a night on a ranch in the Hill Country. The horses are in the corral, and the gate is chained. A boy of fourteen sits by the fence with a rifle, and his older brother will take the next shift. The dog lifts its head at a sound. Everyone listens. It turns out to be a deer. The boy lets out a breath, and the watch goes on. Nights like this came again and again, for years.

The state answered by paying Ranger companies to patrol the frontier. A company might camp near a settlement for weeks, ride out to follow a trail, and ride back. Their presence made some settlers feel safer. But the country was huge, and the Rangers could not be everywhere. A raiding party that knew the ground could usually vanish before they arrived.

Think about what this meant for a family. They had come to build a ranch, raise cattle, and have a quiet life. Instead, they had to keep a loaded gun by the door and a watch over the horses. Frontier ranching was a gamble, and families took it because the land was cheap and the grass was free.

Chapter 3

The Texas Rangers

The Rangers got their start well before statehood. In the 1820s, Stephen F. Austin hired men to guard his colony, and during the Republic the Rangers grew into companies of mounted volunteers. A Ranger usually brought his own horse and gear. The work meant tracking, riding long distances with little food, and knowing the country. The best Rangers were part scout and part soldier.

One of the best-known early leaders was John Coffee Hays, called Jack, a young captain who led Ranger companies out of San Antonio in the 1840s. Hays and his men used a new weapon, the Colt five-shot revolver. Before that, most riders carried guns that fired one shot and took time to reload, which was a bad thing to try on a galloping horse. A revolver let a rider fire several shots without stopping. In 1844, in the Hill Country, Hays and about fifteen Rangers fought a much larger party of Comanche at a place later called Walker’s Creek. Their revolvers helped them hold their own. The story spread, and revolvers became standard gear for frontier riders.

A Ranger company’s day looked a lot like a cowboy’s, with a different purpose. The men rose early, saddled up, checked their guns, and set out on a scout, riding for hours across hills and canyons and reading signs on the ground: hoofprints, trampled grass, the ashes of an old campfire. They slept in the open, ate dried beef and bread, and cooked over small fires. Their horses had to be as tough as any cattle horse, because they might have to run down raiders and then walk home. A Ranger with a worn-out horse was no use to anyone.

In 1858, the state chose a new Ranger captain, John S. “Rip” Ford, to lead a company against raiders. Ford took about a hundred Rangers north, with scouts from allied Native peoples, and found a Comanche camp near the Canadian River, in the area known as the Antelope Hills. The fight lasted for hours, and the Rangers held the field at the end of it. It showed that a Ranger force with good scouts and fast horses could carry the fight into Comanche country, though raids on Texas ranches continued.

Part 3

The Border

Chapter 4Trouble at the River
Chapter 4

Trouble at the River

In 1848, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo fixed the Rio Grande as the boundary between the United States and Mexico. The line was easy to cross. Horses and cattle crossed in both directions, and so did banditry. Texans accused Mexican raiders of stealing their cattle. Mexican ranchers complained about Texans doing the same thing. Cattle with unclear brands made it hard to prove who owned what.

The Rio Grande could be crossed at shallow places called fords, and ranchers on both sides drove cattle across them for grass and water. In a dry year, herds came to the river from miles away and mixed together at the water. Brands were how a rancher told his animals from his neighbor’s, so ranchers on both sides of the river learned to read each other’s marks. Rangers and soldiers watched the crossings, but the river ran for hundreds of miles, and they could not be everywhere.

In 1855, a Ranger leader named James Callahan took about a hundred men across the river after Lipan Apache raiders. They burned part of the Mexican town of Piedras Negras before retreating. Mexico protested.
